results.detail: UNGRADED — needs ground truth from captured store, coverage COMPLETE for this window
results.response:
## Coverage first

All four platforms return `covered` and `complete: true` for Q2 2025 (Apr 1 – Jun 30, 91 days) — Google, Meta, Shopify, GA4. WooCommerce isn't connected. Captured/settled through **2026-08-12**; this is a historical window so there's no live counterpart. The Google live panel is degraded this turn (conversion actions and audiences failed to load) — irrelevant to everything below.

**The honest headline: I can give you two of the three legs cleanly. The third — creative — cannot be closed, and I'll show you exactly why rather than guessing at it.**

There is no captured entity that joins campaign × landing page × creative. Those are three independent rankings from three different families. What lets me connect the first two is not a join key but the tracking parameters sitting inside the landing-page URLs themselves, which carry a Google campaign ID. That's real evidence. The creative leg has no such bridge.

---

# Q2 2025 baseline

| Basis | Revenue | Spend | ROAS |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Shopify (canonical / dashboard card)** | **$117,840.00** | $58,946.14 | **2.00x** |
| GA4 (site-observed) | $115,634.87 | $58,946.14 | 1.96x |
| Google ad-attributed | $147,364.66 | $51,166.07 | 2.88x |
| Meta ad-attributed | $14,913.50 | $7,780.07 | 1.92x |

Store and GA4 sit within 1.9% of each other — unusually tight for this account. The platform-attributed figures are higher because they claim credit on click-date within their own attribution windows; Shopify counts orders on order-date. Google alone claims $147k against a whole-business total of $118k, so its self-reported 2.88x is an attribution ceiling, not a business ROAS.

---

# Leg 1 — Campaign: `Sales-Performance Max-Evergreen`

| Campaign (GA4-attributed) | Revenue | Share of GA4 total |
|---|---|---|
| **Sales-Performance Max-Evergreen** | **$52,757.00** | **45.6%** |
| (direct) | $38,899.00 | 33.6% |
| (referral) | $8,093.33 | 7.0% |
| (organic) | $6,352.00 | 5.5% |
| `{{campaign_name}}` | $2,606.54 | 2.3% |
| (cross-network) | $2,039.00 | 1.8% |
| Meta campaign `120219958226740106` | $592.00 | 0.5% |
| Sales-Search-8 | $324.00 | 0.3% |

**One important caveat on this leg.** Google's own captured campaign family returned a **single unnamed row carrying the entire $51,166.07** — campaign names aren't resolvable on the Google side for this window. So the campaign attribution above is GA4's view, not Google's. It's credible (`google / cpc` totals $53,081 in GA4, and PMax-Evergreen is $52,757 of it — 99.4%), but it rests on one source.

PMax-Evergreen is effectively the entire paid program in Q2 2025. Everything else Google ran was rounding error.

---

# Leg 2 — Landing page: the Original Play Castle Sofa PDP

This one needs un-mangling before it's readable. GA4 returned **74,316 distinct landing-page values** because query strings aren't stripped — the same page is split across dozens of rows by variant ID and tracking params. Collapsing the top 25:

| Page (collapsed) | Revenue in top-25 rows |
|---|---|
| **/products/foamoh-original-play-castle-sofa** | **~$39,984** |
| / (home) | ~$24,485 |
| /products/foamoh-super-castle-play-sofa | ~$6,280 |
| /collections/all | ~$3,549 |

Read at row level, the homepage looks like the winner at $14,650. **Collapsed, the Castle Sofa PDP beats it by roughly 1.6x** — and that's only across the 25 rows I can see out of 74,316.

**This is where the two legs actually connect.** The high-revenue Castle Sofa variants carry `tw_source=google&tw_campaign=20386540795&gad_campaignid=20382323183` in the URL. That is a Google campaign ID stamped on the landing page, and GA4 names the dominant paid campaign as PMax-Evergreen. The path is consistent — though I'd note the ID-to-name mapping isn't in a captured lookup, so it's strong inference, not proof.

**The most interesting page isn't the biggest one.** Super Castle PDP shows $43.23 and $47.75 revenue per key event against $8.94–$19.25 on the Original Castle. Far less traffic, roughly 2.5x the value density.

⚠ GA4 "conversions" here counts **all key events** — add_to_cart, begin_checkout, purchase — not purchases. The `aov` figures the tool derives for GA rows are revenue ÷ key-events and are **not** an average order value. I'm using them only as a relative value-density signal.

---

# Leg 3 — Creative: this cannot be closed, and here's the precise reason

**Google PMax:** no asset-level performance exists. Combinations are empty across every asset group, and the Google asset families aren't backfilled. PMax was 45.6% of revenue and is a black box on creative.

**Meta:** all four asset families returned rows with complete day coverage — but **every single row carries conversions = 0 and conversionValue = 0**. Meta does not attribute conversion value at asset grain in what we hold. So I can rank Meta creative on click economics only. Ranking it on revenue would be inventing a number.

What the click data does say, ranked by CPC within each type:

| Asset | Type | Spend | CTR | CPC |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Stop motion 2 vertical.mov | video | $1,677.16 | 1.37% | $0.32 |
| **cropped_1X1 … Stop motion 2.mov** | video | **$2,675.91** | **0.05%** | **$2.67** |
| untitled_105 | image | $624.83 | 2.84% | $0.18 |
| "Don't wait another minute!" | title | $3,827.21 | 0.22% | $0.77 |
| "FoamOh! is for Life 🎉🇺🇸🌀" | title | $1,619.83 | 2.65% | $0.38 |
| "GROW with FoamOh! ❣️ Purchasing…" | body | $3,209.95 | 0.08% | $1.89 |
| "Investing in a FoamOh!…" | body | $1,258.74 | 2.52% | $0.52 |

The clearest finding in the whole pull: **the same source video, cropped square, cost $2.67/click against $0.32/click vertical — 8.3x worse, and it took the largest video budget in the quarter.** $2,675.91 bought 1,002 clicks; $1,677.16 bought 5,253. Note Meta asset spend is component attribution, not a partition — compare within a type, never sum across types.

Meta conversion counts and CPA are account-level historical figures that are directionally accurate but may not perfectly reconcile with campaign-level numbers; Meta spend, clicks and impressions are exact.

---

# Verdict

**Google PMax `Sales-Performance Max-Evergreen` → `/products/foamoh-original-play-castle-sofa` was the best full-funnel path in Q2 2025** — roughly $52.8k GA4-attributed revenue through a landing page carrying that campaign's ID, ~45.6% of all site revenue. The creative that closed those sales is **not knowable**, because PMax exposes no asset performance and the 13% of spend that ran on Meta has no conversion value at asset grain.

Three things I'd act on:

1. **Strip query parameters in GA4.** 74,316 landing-page values for what is realistically a few dozen pages. Every page-level read you take is understated until this is fixed, and it's a config change, not an analysis problem.
2. **`{{campaign_name}}` is an unrendered template macro** sitting in your UTMs — $2,606.54 and 701 key events landed in a literal placeholder string. Something is publishing ads with the variable un-interpolated.
3. **Meta's GA4-observed revenue was ~$3,792** (`facebook/paid` + `ig/paid` + `fb/paid`) against Meta's own claim of $14,913.50 — a 3.9x gap on $7,780 of spend. Worth resolving before any judgement about Meta's Q2 2025 performance, in either direction.

If you want the creative leg genuinely closed going forward, the fix is upstream of me: Meta asset-level conversion reporting, and accepting that PMax will never give it to you.

| Store ROAS | 1.95x | **3.27x** | +68% |
| GA4 revenue | $255,097.58 | $69,688.29 | −72.7% |
| GA4 ROAS | 1.83x | 3.12x | +70% |

The efficiency gain is real but it is a **composition effect, not a skill effect** — blended ROAS rose because the denominator collapsed while organic revenue kept flowing. The four months that actually ran paid media (Jan–Apr) delivered a blended MER around **1.6x**, and that is the honest number for what the media was doing when it was on.

Two ROAS bases differ above because they measure different things: store ROAS is order-date revenue from Shopify divided by ad spend; GA4 ROAS is click-attributed, session-scoped revenue on GA4's model. Ad-attributed ROAS (2.61x in the 2025 window, 1.29x YTD 2026) is the platforms' own conversionValue and credits only what they claim — a third basis again.

**On the Meta / Andromeda question.** I want to be straight rather than agreeable here: I can't test that narrative from this pull, and the shape of the data pushes back on it. Meta ad-attributed ROAS across Jan–Aug 2025 was **2.97x** ($44,202.81 spend → $131,294.30 attributed value) — not obviously broken. More to the point, **Meta has spent $0 since October 2025**, so there is no post-period spend in which ROAS could have "failed to recover." The account didn't fail to recover; it stopped running. If you want that belief properly tested, the pull is a Meta month-by-month series through 2024–2025 — I'll run it on request. (Meta account-level conversion counts and CPA are directionally accurate but may not reconcile perfectly with campaign-level numbers; spend, clicks and impressions are exact.)

---

# 2. Shopify — small, healthy, concentrated

**Live** (provisional, as-of 2026-08-14): net sales **$989.00**, **5 orders**, AOV **$197.80**.
**Captured** (settled through 2026-08-12): store revenue **$989.00**. The two agree exactly.

Money waterfall, `shopify_current_refundAdjusted` basis, coverage complete on all 29 days:

| Component | Jul 15 – Aug 13 |
|---|---|
| Gross sales | $1,004.00 |
| − Discounts | $15.00 |
| = Net sales | **$989.00** |
| + Taxes | $15.54 |
| + Shipping | $0.00 |
| + Tips | $0.00 |
| = Total sales | $1,004.54 |
| − Refunds | $0.00 |

Payment fees, cart tax, shipping tax and discount tax were **not captured on any of the 29 days** — that's "not captured," not $0, so I can't give you a fee-net figure.

Signals worth noting at this volume, with the caveat that 5 orders is a sample, not a trend:
- **Discount rate 1.5%** of gross and **shipping revenue $0** — full-price selling, free shipping absorbed.
- **Zero refunds, zero refund rate.**
- **Product concentration is extreme**: FoamOh Original Play Castle Sofa is **$762 of $989 — 77%** of revenue, 3 units. Everything else is attach (cover set $109, steps $49, ramp $49, pillow $20).
- **New-customer AOV $214 vs returning $133**, 20% returning-order rate. Returning customers are buying accessories, not second sofas — expected for a durable-goods category, but it caps LTV, which matters when you rebuild paid.
- **1 abandoned checkout against 5 orders.** Full funnel isn't API-exposed so I won't quote a rate.

---

# 3. GA4 — the site is still getting traffic, and it's leaking

1,941 sessions, 1,548 users, engagement rate 55.80%, **6 transactions**, $1,098 revenue.

**The funnel, and this is the finding:**

| Step | Events | Step conversion |
|---|---|---|
| add_to_cart | 187 | — |
| begin_checkout | 69 | 36.9% |
| add_payment_info | 10 | **14.5%** |
| purchase | 6 | 60.0% |

Cart-to-purchase **3.21%**; purchaser conversion rate **0.39%**. The break is unambiguous: **begin_checkout → add_payment_info loses 85.5%** of the funnel. Fifty-nine people opened checkout and never reached the payment step. On a $198 AOV that's the highest-value single fix available, and it costs nothing in media. Check shipping-cost reveal, checkout field friction, and mobile checkout specifically — mobile is 60.3% of sessions (1,170 of 1,941).

**Traffic composition (captured, coverage COMPLETE on all 29 days):**

| Channel | Sessions | Conv. | Revenue |
|---|---|---|---|
| Direct | 837 | 103 | $617 |
| Organic Search | 804 | 111 | $348 |
| Organic Shopping | — | 21 | $133 |
| AI Assistant | 13 | 18 | $0 |
| Paid Search | 75 | 0 | $0 |
| Unassigned | — | 68 | $0 |

Three things here:

1. **95.9% of users are new** (1,485 of 1,548) — only 63 returning. With zero retargeting running, there is no mechanism recapturing the 187 people who added to cart. That is a structural hole, not a performance one.
2. **75 `google / cpc` sessions with $0 Google Ads spend.** Those sessions are real but the medium tag is wrong — almost certainly Merchant Center free listings or a stale UTM inheriting a paid label. Worth fixing before you restart paid, or your first month of Google reporting will be contaminated.
3. **`chatgpt.com / ai-assistant`: 13 sessions, 18 conversions.** Tiny, but it's the highest conversion-per-session source on the list and it's a channel that didn't exist in your 2024 baseline. Worth watching.

**Traffic quality caveat:** 1,722 of 1,941 sessions are US (88.7%). The remaining 219 include Romania (33), India (29), China (12), Vietnam (8), Mauritius (7) — for a US-only service area that's likely bot/noise inflating your session denominator and depressing your conversion rates by roughly a tenth.

**Landing pages:** the homepage does 767 sessions at **4.56%** session conv rate, while the Castle Sofa PDP does 136 at **1.47%** and every collections page converts at **0.00%**. Your homepage is outselling your product pages by 3x. That inverts the usual pattern and says the PDPs are underbuilt.

---

# 4. GA4 vs Shopify reconciliation

GA4 $1,098 / 6 transactions vs Shopify $989 net / 5 orders. Delta **−$109 (−11.0%)**, one transaction.

This is a basis difference, not an error: Shopify net sales is refund-adjusted and **excludes shipping and tax**; GA4 purchase revenue includes tax and is session-attributed on click date, so an order placed near a window edge lands in different buckets. Note the direction flips period to period — in the prior 30 days (Jun 14 – Jul 13) store revenue was **$1,279** against GA4's **$578**, i.e. GA4 *under*-reported by 55%. That instability at 5–6 orders/month is sample noise, but it means neither source should be treated as authoritative at this volume. Shopify is the money; GA4 is the behaviour.

---

# 5. Scorecard

| Area | State | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Google Ads | 🔴 Dark | $0 since May 2026; 43 campaigns all paused |
| Meta Ads | 🔴 Dark | $0 since Oct 2025 |
| Shopify | 🟡 Healthy but tiny | 5 orders, $989, zero refunds, 77% single-SKU |
| GA4 traffic | 🟢 Holding | 1,941 sessions, 55.8% engagement, no paid support |
| Checkout funnel | 🔴 Broken | 85.5% loss at begin_checkout → add_payment_info |
| Retention | 🔴 Absent | 95.9% new users, no retargeting running |
| Tracking hygiene | 🟡 | 75 phantom `google/cpc` sessions; 11% non-US traffic |
| Data capture | 🟢 Clean | All 4 platforms `covered`, live=captured this window |

---

# 6. What I'd do, in order

1. **Fix the checkout payment-step drop before spending another dollar.** 59 lost sessions at that stage, at a $198 AOV, is the cheapest revenue in the account. Restarting paid media into a checkout that loses 85.5% of initiated orders just buys the leak more volume.
2. **Clean the `google/cpc` mis-tag and add a bot/geo filter** so the restart baseline is measurable.
3. **Stand up retargeting before prospecting.** 187 add-to-carts a month with zero recapture is free inventory.
4. **Rebuild the PDPs** — the homepage converting at 3x the Castle Sofa product page, and collections at 0%, is the clearest on-site diagnosis in this dataset.
5. **Then restart paid, small and Google-first,** on the Castle Sofa only. It's 77% of revenue and it's what the 2026 spend was already supporting.

**The one thing still blocking a verdict on step 5:** I've flagged this before and it hasn't landed yet — **COGS / contribution margin**. At March's blended MER of 1.66x, breakeven sits at roughly **60% contribution margin**. Above that, restarting Google at April/March levels made money and pausing it was the error. Below it, the pause was correct and you should restart at a much lower budget with a strict target. I cannot resolve that from captured data because we don't capture cost of goods — it has to come from you.

results.message: Meta, GA4 and Shopify all count the same purchases differently for Q2 2025 — explain the three numbers.
results.detail: UNGRADED — needs ground truth from captured store, coverage COMPLETE for this window
results.response:
All four platforms returned `covered` and `complete: true` for 2025-04-01 → 2025-06-30. Captured store, settled through **2026-08-12**. Q2 2025 is historical, so there's no live counterpart to place beside it — the live panel in this view is July 2026. Google's live panel is degraded this turn (conversion actions and audiences failed to load); nothing below depends on it.

---

# The three numbers

| Source | Purchase count | Revenue | What it's actually measuring |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Shopify** | **559 orders** | **$117,840.00** net sales | Every order the business took, order-date, refund-adjusted |
| **GA4** | *not readable* — see below | **$115,634.87** | Purchase events fired by a tagged, consenting browser |
| **Meta** | **70 purchases** | **$14,913.50** | Orders Meta claims credit for, dated to the ad touch |

These aren't three attempts at one number. They're answers to three different questions, and only Shopify is answering "how many orders did we take."

---

## 1. Shopify — 559 orders, $117,840. This is the denominator.

Full waterfall, `shopify_current_refundAdjusted`, all 91 days present:

| Component | Q2 2025 |
|---|---|
| Gross sales | $121,067.00 |
| − Discounts | $1,993.00 |
| **= Net sales (pre-tax/ship)** | **$119,074.00** |
| + Taxes | $2,538.24 |
| + Shipping | $150.00 |
| + Tips | $0.00 |
| = Total sales | $120,528.24 |
| − Refunds | $364.00 |
| **= Net sales (reported)** | **$117,840.00** |

Fees, cart tax, shipping tax and discount tax are `null` on all 91 days — not captured, not $0. AOV is **$210.81** on 559 distinct orders.

This is the only one of the three that is a count of orders. It doesn't care whether the customer was cookied, consented, or ever saw an ad.

## 2. GA4 — $115,634.87, and I can't give you a transaction count

**The revenue figure is solid: $115,634.87.** The purchase *count* is not something I can hand you for this window. The account-grain conversions figure is **8,151**, but that's every key event GA4 counts — add_to_cart, begin_checkout, form_submit, the lot — not transactions. I pulled the `ga_event` family twice (ranked by conversions and by revenue) and it returned all 16 event names including `purchase`, coverage `COMPLETE` on all 91 days, but every metric column came back zero — the event-count values aren't populated in that family's stored columns. That's a gap on our side in what got written, not evidence that GA4 recorded no purchases. I'm not going to derive a count by dividing revenue by an AOV from a different system and present it as GA4's number.

On the revenue, the comparison depends on which Shopify line you hold it against, and this matters:

- vs Shopify **net sales** ($117,840): GA4 is **−$2,205.13, −1.9%**
- vs Shopify **total sales** ($120,528.24): GA4 is **−$4,893.37, −4.1%**

The second is the more honest like-for-like if your GA4 purchase event passes tax and shipping (standard Shopify GA4 setup does). And note two errors running in opposite directions: Shopify's net is refund-adjusted, GA4's never is — the $364 of refunds sits inside GA4's figure and got stripped from Shopify's. So GA4's true tracking loss is a bit worse than the headline 1.9% suggests. A 2–4% shortfall is normal browser attrition — consent declines, ad-blockers, ITP, users who bounce before the tag fires.

## 3. Meta — 70 purchases, $14,913.50. A claim, not a count.

Meta reports 70 purchases on **$7,780.07** of spend — a **1.92x** ad-attributed ROAS, **$111.14** CPA. That's **12.5% of the 559 orders** and **12.7% of net sales**.

Three things about that 70:

**It appears six times under six labels.** `purchase`, `omni_purchase`, `offsite_conversion.fb_pixel_purchase`, `onsite_web_purchase`, `onsite_web_app_purchase` and `web_in_store_purchase` all read exactly 70 / $14,913.50. That's one event wearing six names — never sum them.

**It's dated to the ad touch, not the order.** Shopify books an order on the day money moved. Meta books it on the day of the click or impression that preceded it, within its attribution window. Orders placed in early April off a late-March ad land in Q1 for Meta and Q2 for Shopify. On a 91-day window that's a small edge effect, but it's real.

**Its per-order value is $213.05** ($14,913.50 ÷ 70) — sitting between Shopify's net AOV of $210.81 and total-sales AOV of $215.62. So the pixel is passing roughly the correct order value. The divergence between Meta and Shopify is entirely in *which orders get claimed*, not in how an order is valued.

One brief note per our data source: Meta conversion counts and CPA here are account-level historical figures — directionally accurate but they may not perfectly reconcile with campaign-level conversion numbers. Meta spend, clicks and impressions are exact.

---

# The cleanest illustration of the gap

GA4 assigns **Paid Social** a revenue of **$3,950.54** in Q2 2025. Meta claims **$14,913.50** for the same quarter.

**Meta claims 3.8x what GA4 gives it.** Nothing is broken. GA4 is last-non-direct, click-only, cookie-scoped — a user who saw a Meta ad, didn't click, searched the brand two days later and bought gets credited to Organic Search. Meta counts that same order as its own via view-through, plus it stitches across devices using logged-in identity that GA4's cookie can't follow.

That $10,963 gap is the entire argument about Meta's contribution, expressed as a number. Neither figure is the truth: GA4's $3,950 is the floor (click-only), Meta's $14,913 is the ceiling (self-reported, view-through included). The real contribution is somewhere between, and no captured platform can tell you where — only a holdout test can.

---

# One thing worth flagging while we're on measurement basis

Google reports **$147,364.67** of conversion value on $51,166.07 of spend in Q2 2025. The store took **$117,840** in total, from all sources combined. Google alone is claiming **1.25x the entire business's revenue**. That's not a Google-vs-Shopify version of the same 2–4% tracking discrepancy — it's a different order of problem, and the usual cause is multiple conversion actions counted as primary (purchase plus begin_checkout plus a lead form, all with values attached).

I'd want to confirm that against the conversion-action breakdown before calling it. That family's live fetch failed this turn, and separately it's forward-only in our store — the first row anywhere is 2026-06-27, so there is no captured conversion-action detail for Q2 2025 at all. Absence there is correct and expected, not a gap. The 2026 data would tell us whether the double-counting is structural, and if it is, it was almost certainly structural in Q2 2025 too.

Want me to pull the 2026 conversion-action split to test that?

results.message: Which platform actually drove growth in Q2 2025? Defend it with three independent sources.
results.detail: UNGRADED — needs ground truth from captured store, coverage COMPLETE for this window
results.response:
All four platforms return `covered` and `complete: true` for every window below — Google, Meta, Shopify, GA4. WooCommerce isn't connected. Everything is captured/settled through **2026-08-12**; these are historical quarters, so there's no live counterpart to show alongside them. The Google live panel is degraded this turn (conversion actions and audiences failed to load) — nothing in this analysis depends on either.

---

# Verdict

**Google. It isn't close, and the three sources agree independently.**

But first, a definition problem you should hold onto: **Q2 2025 only grew sequentially, not year-over-year.**

| | Q2 2024 | Q1 2025 | Q2 2025 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Store revenue (Shopify net) | $126,988.74 | $69,400.30 | **$117,840.00** |
| Orders | 574 | 318 | **559** |
| Total ad spend | $46,978.54 | $50,963.20 | **$58,946.14** |
| Blended MER (store ÷ spend) | 2.70x | 1.36x | **2.00x** |

Against Q1 2025 that's **+$48,439.70 revenue (+69.8%) and +241 orders (+75.8%)** on only **+$7,982.94 more spend (+15.7%)** — MER 1.36x → 2.00x. Against Q2 2024 it's **−7.2% revenue on +25.5% spend**. So "growth in Q2 2025" is a real, large sequential recovery, and I'll defend Google as its driver — but it is a recovery toward the 2024 line, not a breakout past it.

---

# The control first: Q1→Q2 is normally a *decline* for this account

This is what makes the sequential number worth anything.

| Q1 → Q2 | Change in store revenue |
|---|---|
| 2023 | $14,665.06 → $12,299.75 = **−16.1%** |
| 2024 | $193,524.00 → $126,988.74 = **−34.4%** |
| **2025** | $69,400.30 → $117,840.00 = **+69.8%** |

Both prior years fell into Q2. 2025 rose 70%. Whatever drove Q2 2025 was strong enough to invert the account's own seasonal shape — so this is not "Q2 is just a good quarter."

---

# Source 1 — Google Ads' own attribution (platform-reported)

| Google | Q1 2025 | Q2 2025 | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Spend | $14,964.01 | $51,166.07 | **+$36,202.06 (+242%)** |
| Impressions | 1,398,279 | 3,916,669 | +180% |
| Clicks | 11,461 | 29,956 | +161% |
| Conversions | 255.4 | 681.7 | **+167%** |
| Ad-attributed value | $61,085.98 | $147,364.67 | **+$86,278.69 (+141%)** |
| Ad-ROAS (platform basis) | 4.08x | 2.88x | −29% |

Google was scaled **3.4x** and returned +141% in its own attributed value. This is the weakest of the three sources on its own — it's Google marking its own homework, and PMax in particular absorbs credit generously. It only counts because of what follows.

---

# Source 2 — GA4, independent tag-based measurement (last non-direct click)

Different vendor, different attribution model, different collection mechanism. It agrees.

| GA4 source / medium | Q1 2025 revenue | Q2 2025 revenue | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| **google / cpc** | $19,364.20 | **$53,081.00** | **+$33,716.80 (+174%)** |
| (direct) / (none) | $30,415.10 | $38,899.00 | +$8,483.90 (+28%) |
| google / organic | $4,880.00 | $5,401.00 | +$10.7% |
| **facebook / paid** | $4,319.00 | **$1,384.00** | **−$2,935.00 (−68%)** |

Breakdown coverage: **COMPLETE** on all 91/91 and 90/90 active days for both quarters.

Two things here. First, GA4's *total* revenue moved $67,895.71 → $115,634.87 (**+70.3%**), which independently reproduces Shopify's +69.8% — two separate systems measuring the same quarter within 1.9% of each other, which is why I'll lean on both. Second, **google/cpc alone accounts for $33,717 of the $47,739 GA4 revenue increase — 71% of all measured growth, from a single channel.** Meanwhile paid social went the other way.

The Q2 GA4 channel split confirms where it landed: **Cross-network $54,796** (the PMax bucket) vs **Paid Social $3,950.54**. Google surfaces carry 14x the paid social revenue.

One caveat on this source: Direct also grew +$8,484, and some share of that is untagged Google-driven traffic (halo, dark clicks) — which would make Google's contribution *larger*, not smaller. I'm not claiming it; I'm flagging that the error runs one direction.

---

# Source 3 — Shopify, the money itself (no attribution at all)

This source can't tell you *who* drove growth, so I'm using it to prove *what kind* of growth it was — which rules out the alternative explanations.

| Shopify | Q1 2025 | Q2 2025 |
|---|---|---|
| Net revenue | $69,400.30 | $117,840.00 |
| Orders | 318 | **559** |
| AOV | $218.24 | $210.81 (**−3.4%**) |

Growth was **entirely unit-driven**: +241 orders with AOV flat-to-slightly-down. So it was not a price rise, not a mix shift into expensive SKUs, and not a handful of large orders. It required ~76% more buyers, which requires more qualified traffic — and Q2's incremental traffic came from one place.

Channel split confirms it landed on-site, not on a marketplace: **web $108,382 (92% of revenue, 508 of 559 orders)**, Amazon $6,768, Shop $1,339, Facebook channel $863, TikTok $199. So no marketplace surge is hiding in there. Coverage COMPLETE.

---

# The counterfactual, which is the strongest evidence of all

Meta was **cut 78% in the same quarter** — $35,999.19 → $7,780.07, a **−$28,219.12** reduction — and revenue rose 70% anyway.

| Meta | Q1 2025 | Q2 2025 |
|---|---|---|
| Spend | $35,999.19 | $7,780.07 |
| Impressions | 7,049,315 | 2,687,306 |
| Conversions | 770 | 70 |
| Ad-attributed value | $116,380.80 | $14,913.50 |
| Ad-ROAS | 3.23x | 1.92x |

Meta cannot be the growth driver — it was the *funding source*. Roughly $28.2K moved out of Meta and $36.2K moved into Google, net +$8.0K, and the store took +$48.4K. That is the whole quarter in one sentence.

*(Meta account-level conversion counts and CPA here are historical account-grain figures — directionally accurate but they won't reconcile perfectly with campaign-level numbers; Meta spend, clicks and impressions are exact.)*

Worth noting for your Andromeda read: Meta's ad-ROAS did fall 3.23x → 1.92x here, but at $7,780 of spend across a 78% budget cut, that quarter can't separate "audience quality degraded" from "spend collapsed below the level where delivery works." It's consistent with your hypothesis; it isn't evidence for it.

---

# What I would not claim

- **Efficiency deteriorated while Google scaled.** Ad-ROAS 4.08x → 2.88x on 3.4x the budget. The incremental $36,202 bought $86,279 of attributed value — a **marginal ad-ROAS of 2.38x**, well under the 4.08x Q1 base. Growth was bought at a declining rate of return, which matters if you're deciding whether to push further.
- **I could not get per-campaign Google rows back this turn** — the campaign-level query returned window totals only (137 campaign-rows exist in Q2, but no per-campaign detail came back). So I can't tell you *which* Google campaigns took the $36K. That's the obvious next pull and it's the one that turns this into an action.
- **Whether Google was incremental or harvesting.** All three sources show Google *captured* the growth. None of them can prove it *created* it. The +28% Direct growth and +11% organic growth in the same quarter suggest some underlying demand lift that Google would have caught either way.
- **Profit.** Still no COGS. At $210.81 AOV and 2.00x blended MER, whether this quarter made money depends on a number only you have — same blocker as the year-over-year work.

---

# What I'd do with this

1. **Pull the Google campaign split for Q2 2025** — PMax vs Search vs Shopping. GA4 puts $54,796 in Cross-network, which is PMax-dominated; if PMax took most of the $36K increment, the 2.38x marginal return is a PMax scaling curve and you can model where it flattens.
2. **Test the reallocation, don't assume it's permanent.** Q2 2025 still sits 7.2% below Q2 2024 revenue on 25.5% more spend. The Meta-to-Google shift beat Q1, but the 2024 structure beat both.
3. **Get Direct honest.** $38,899 through (direct)/(none) — 34% of GA4 revenue — is the single largest attribution hole, and it's the difference between Google driving 71% of growth and Google driving more.

---

# The short answer, and it isn't a scale-up story

**Q3 2024 Google spend was $1,816.71. Q3 2025 was $53,107.04 — a 29x increase.** But the account didn't grow. It swapped channels: Meta went from **$114,680.56** to **$2,988.45** over the same two quarters. Total media spend actually *halved*.

## Google, Q3 2024 → Q3 2025

| Metric | Q3 2024 | Q3 2025 | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Spend | $1,816.71 | **$53,107.04** | **+$51,290 (+2,823%)** |
| Impressions | 237,707 | 4,352,724 | +18.3x |
| Clicks | 6,411 | 34,955 | +5.5x |
| CTR | 2.70% | 0.80% | −70% |
| CPC | $0.28 | $1.52 | +443% |
| Conversions | 567.2 | 589.8 | **+4.0%** |
| CPA | $3.20 | $90.04 | +2,714% |
| Ad-attributed conv. value | $127,036.58 | $130,415.47 | **+2.7%** |
| Ad-attributed ROAS | 69.93x | 2.46x | — |

**That table has one line that should stop you: conversions and conversion value are essentially flat while spend went up 29-fold.** $51,290 of incremental Google spend bought 22.6 additional conversions and $3,379 of additional ad-attributed value.

I'd treat the Q3 2024 side sceptically before concluding "we destroyed a 70x channel." A 69.93x ad-ROAS on $1,816 with 567 conversions off 6,411 clicks (8.85% conversion rate) is not a plausible paid-search performance figure — it's the signature of a conversion action set crediting Google for demand it didn't create (free listings, brand, or an all-conversions column carrying non-paid credit). The near-identical value in both years, at wildly different spend, is the tell: that value isn't spend-elastic, so it wasn't spend-driven.

I can't confirm which conversion actions were firing in either quarter — the `conversion_action` family has no backfill in our store (first row anywhere is 2026-06-27), and its live fetch also failed this turn. So that diagnosis is a read of the shape of the numbers, not a verified account fact.

## The whole account, same two quarters

| Metric | Q3 2024 | Q3 2025 | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Google spend | $1,816.71 | $53,107.04 | +2,823% |
| Meta spend | $114,680.56 | $2,988.45 | −97.4% |
| **Total media spend** | **$116,497.27** | **$56,095.49** | **−51.8%** |
| Shopify revenue (store) | $220,698.19 | $172,350.40 | −21.9% |
| **Blended ROAS (store)** | **1.89x** | **3.07x** | **+62%** |
| GA4 revenue | $262,966.34 | $147,002.40 | −44.1% |
| Blended ROAS (GA4 basis) | 2.26x | 2.62x | +16% |

Both revenue sources are shown because both are present. **Shopify is the canonical figure** — it's order-date, refund-adjusted, and matches the dashboard cards. GA4 is session-attributed and credits revenue to the click, on a different window and a different measurement basis, so the two never tie exactly.

**What's notable is the direction flip.** In Q3 2024 GA4 read *$42,268 higher* than Shopify (+19%). In Q3 2025 it read *$25,348 lower* (−15%). GA4 didn't just fall — it fell 44% while actual orders fell 22%, meaning roughly half of GA4's decline is measurement loss, not business loss. That's the same identification break flagged earlier in this account.

---

# What actually changed

**You cut spend 52% and revenue fell 22%.** Blended efficiency improved from 1.89x to 3.07x. On media math alone that's a good trade — you gave up $48,348 of revenue to save $60,402 of spend.

**But the channel you scaled into isn't the one carrying it.** Google absorbed nearly all of Q3 2025's budget and returned $130,415 of ad-attributed value against $172,350 of actual store revenue. Meta at $2,988 returned $10,440 — a 3.49x ad-attributed ROAS on the residue, *higher* than the 2.20x Meta was doing at $114,680 in Q3 2024. That's a small, non-representative sample and I wouldn't build a plan on it, but it doesn't support a reading in which Meta's efficiency was permanently broken — the spend left before the efficiency did.

**And organic is doing more work than the paid numbers admit.** Q3 2024 delivered $220,698 of store revenue on effectively no Google spend. That baseline is the number to hold the 2025 Google investment against — not zero.

---

# Where I'd take this

The comparison that would settle it is **Q3 2025 Google monthly**, to see whether the 29x ramp had a working month before it flattened, or whether it was inefficient from the first dollar. That's a direct read on whether the Google scale-up is fixable or should be unwound.

The COGS number I've asked for twice is still the blocker on the verdict itself. At Q3 2025's spend and revenue, the swap made money on media; whether it made money on *contribution* depends entirely on margin, and that figure only exists on your side.

One live-panel note that touches nothing above: Google audiences failed to load this turn, and Google deep-history backfill and interior gap repair are paused by choice while the capture engine is completed. Both Q3 windows are fully captured and unaffected.

# Neither. Both got less efficient on every measure but one.

| | Google Q2'24 | Google Q2'25 | Δ | Meta Q2'24 | Meta Q2'25 | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Spend | $12,591 | $51,166 | +306% | $34,387 | $7,780 | −77% |
| Conversions | 450.5 | 681.7 | +51% | 1,079 | 70 | −94% |
| **CPA** | **$27.95** | **$75.06** | **+169%** | **$31.87** | **$111.14** | **+249%** |
| CTR | 1.03% | 0.76% | −26% | 1.13% | 0.51% | −55% |
| CPC | $1.21 | $1.71 | +41% | $0.46 | $0.57 | +24% |
| CPM | $12.48 | $13.06 | +5% | $5.18 | **$2.90** | **−44%** |
| Click→conv rate | 4.34% | 2.28% | −47% | 1.44% | 0.51% | −65% |
| Ad-attributed ROAS | 8.74x | 2.88x | −67% | 6.68x | 1.92x | −71% |

**If you're forcing a ranking: Google degraded less** — CPA +169% vs Meta's +249%, ad-ROAS −67% vs −71%. But that's a comparison between two different *kinds* of degradation, and the direction matters more than the magnitude.

**Google's is the ordinary shape of scaling.** It took 4.1x the budget and returned 1.5x the conversions. That's a textbook diminishing-returns curve — you bought further down the demand pool, CPC rose 41%, conversion rate halved. Unwelcome, entirely explicable, and reversible by pulling spend back down the curve.

**Meta's is the worrying shape, because it went the wrong way.** Spend was cut 77%. Cutting budget normally *improves* efficiency — you retain the best-converting pockets and shed the marginal ones. Instead CPA nearly tripled and click→conv rate fell 65%. Efficiency deteriorating *while* you shrink is not a diminishing-returns story; something in delivery or conversion quality changed independently of budget.

# The one metric that improved anywhere

**Meta CPM fell 44%**, $5.18 → $2.90. Cheaper impressions, but CTR more than halved alongside it — so Meta was serving into materially cheaper, materially less responsive inventory. That combination is what a delivery-quality shift looks like, and it's the strongest piece of evidence in this window for your Andromeda read.

It is still not proof. A 77% budget cut is exactly the condition under which Meta drops you into cheap remnant inventory anyway — the two explanations produce the same fingerprint here, and Q2-vs-Q2 alone cannot separate them. What separates them is **whether CPM and CTR broke before or after the budget came down**. That's a month-by-month Meta pull across the cut, and I can run it whenever you want it — it's the single cleanest test available on this account.

# Read the ROAS collapse carefully

The two platforms *claimed* $339.6k of conversion value in Q2 2024 against $127.0k of actual store revenue — a **2.67x overclaim**. In Q2 2025 they claimed $162.3k against $117.8k — a **1.38x overclaim**.

So the platforms' own ROAS numbers fell ~70% while real store revenue fell **7%**. A large share of that apparent collapse is the attribution basis tightening on both platforms simultaneously, not performance evaporating. Don't take 8.74x → 2.88x at face value as a business outcome.

**The only efficiency figure anchored to real money is blended MER: 2.70x → 2.00x.** That's the honest measure of the quarter, it's a genuine 26% deterioration, and it's the one to hold both platforms to. Neither platform improved on it; the mix simply moved to the more expensive one.

Meta account-level conversion counts and CPA above are directionally accurate but may not reconcile perfectly with campaign-level figures; Meta spend, clicks and impressions are exact.

results.response:
## Short answer: no — but only ~$400 of the ~$1,900 gap is real

Q2 2026 (2026-04-01 → 06-30), captured store, all four platforms `covered`, `complete: true`, settled through **2026-08-12**. Both are historical windows, so there's no live counterpart to show alongside them.

| Source | Q2 2026 revenue | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| **Shopify — net sales** | **$9,906.00** | after refunds, excludes tax & shipping |
| Shopify — total sales | $10,144.78 | after refunds, includes tax & shipping |
| Shopify — gross sales | $11,227.00 | before discounts & refunds |
| **GA4 — revenue** | **$11,843.00** | purchase-event value, includes tax & shipping, **refund-blind** |

Face-value delta: GA4 is **+$1,937 (+19.6%)** over Shopify net sales.

## Where the gap actually goes

The two aren't measuring the same quantity, and three of the four differences are mechanical:

| Step | Amount |
|---|---|
| Shopify net sales | $9,906.00 |
| + Taxes | $163.78 |
| + Shipping | $75.00 |
| + Refunds added back (GA4 never removes them) | $1,295.11 |
| **= Shopify on a GA4-comparable basis** | **≈ $11,439.89** |
| GA4 reported | $11,843.00 |
| **Unexplained residual** | **+$403.11 (+3.5%)** |

So **~79% of the gap is refunds**, another ~12% is tax and shipping, and only **$403 — 3.5% — is genuine measurement disagreement.** For GA4 vs a client-side purchase tag, 3.5% over a quarter is normal-to-good; it's the direction you'd expect from GA4 double-firing a purchase event on a reload or a thank-you-page revisit. It is *not* a tracking break.

Two caveats on my own arithmetic: the Shopify waterfall reconciles to within **$34.11** (gross − discounts − refunds = $9,871.89 vs the reported $9,906 net), which is refund allocation across tax/shipping rather than product, and **fees, cart tax, shipping tax and discount tax were not captured on any of the 91 days** — null, not $0. Neither is large enough to move the verdict.

## The thing worth acting on

**Refunds were $1,295.11 on $11,227 gross — 11.5% of gross sales in Q2.** GA4 is structurally blind to that, so every channel-level revenue and ROAS figure you read out of GA4 is overstated by roughly that much. That's the real finding here, not the reconciliation.

Both revenue sources against Q2 ad spend of **$3,230.89** (Google only — Meta was $0 all quarter, consistent with it being dark since 2025-10-01):

- **Store basis (the dashboard card): $9,906 ÷ $3,230.89 = 3.07x**
- GA basis: $11,843 ÷ $3,230.89 = 3.67x

The 0.60x spread between those is the same refund-and-tax difference, not a different attribution story. **Use 3.07x for anything that touches the P&L; use GA4 only for channel mix.**

This is the same pattern the live last-30-day panel shows — GA4 $1,098 vs Shopify net $989, GA4 higher by 11% — so the relationship is stable, not a Q2 anomaly.

Worth pulling next if useful: what's driving an 11.5% refund rate, by product. The Castle Sofa is carrying most of the revenue, and if it's also carrying most of the refunds that changes the contribution-margin picture I've flagged before.

## Yes — but read it carefully

**"bath fitters" logged 58.99 conversions in July on $8,649.60, a $146.62 CPA.** That's real captured conversion data (settled through 2026-08-12, coverage COMPLETE across all 31 active days), not a zero or a gap. Three things qualify that number, though.

**1. Those "conversions" are form fills, not jobs.** The `ROAS 0.00x` next to it isn't a failure — there's no revenue source wired to this account at all (no store connected, GA4 revenue is $0), so ROAS literally cannot be computed. The `conversionValue` of $30.49 is a nominal per-conversion weight Google is carrying, not money. For an offline-sales business this is expected; the real question is lead→sold rate, which lives in your CRM, not here.

**2. The account is almost certainly counting each lead twice.** I pulled the conversion-action breakdown from the captured store (the live fetch for that family errored this turn, so this is the captured figure). July, account-wide, has exactly two actions feeding the Conversions column:

| Conversion action | July conversions |
|---|---|
| MyBathFitterUSA.com (web) lp_form_submission | 341.61 |
| bathfitterjersey.com – GA4 (web) contact_form_submission | 303.73 |
| **Total** | **645.34** |

That total matches July's 645 account conversions exactly, and the two actions track at a near-constant ~1.12:1 ratio in every single campaign. Two separate form-submission trackers moving in lockstep on the same lead flow is the signature of one event counted on two systems — a landing-page conversion plus a GA4-imported version of the same submission.

If that's what's happening, **"bath fitters" produced roughly 30 unique leads, not 59, and its true CPA is closer to $275–$290, not $146.** That's a materially different verdict on the account's single most expensive keyword. ## Q2 2026 vs Q2 2021 — Influential Drones

Both windows come back **complete** on the platforms that existed then. Two coverage facts first, because they shape the comparison:

- **GA4** — we have no captured GA4 data before **2023-06-22**, so there is no Q2 2021 site-analytics side. That is not zero, it's outside our floor.
- **Meta** — no captured Meta data before **2024-09-17**, same story. (In Q2 2026 Meta *is* covered and shows a genuine **$0 spend** — real, not missing.)

So the like-for-like spine is **Shopify + Google Ads**.

### Headline

| | Q2 2021 | Q2 2026 | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Store revenue (Shopify, canonical) | $149,135.49 | **$403,353.05** | **+170.5%** (+$254,218) |
| Google ad spend | $461.41 | $4,107.85 | +790% |
| Store ROAS (rev ÷ ad spend) | 323.22× | 98.19× | — |
| Google impressions | 153,383 | 17,016 | −88.9% |
| Google clicks | 995 | 870 | −12.6% |
| Google CTR | 0.65% | 5.11% | +4.46 pts |
| Google CPC | $0.46 | $4.72 | +926% |
| Google ad-attributed conv. value | $1,364.00 | **$3.00** | −99.8% |

GA4 adds a second revenue lens for Q2 2026 only: **$36,559.63** (GA ROAS 8.90× on Google spend). It's ~9% of the Shopify figure because GA4 only credits sessions it can tag and tie to a purchase event, while Shopify counts every order regardless of origin — including phone, quote, and offline-closed deals, which is where the bulk of this account's money now sits.

### What actually changed

**The business grew; the media didn't grow with it.** Revenue is up 2.7× on ad spend that is still trivial in absolute terms ($4.1k in a quarter). The ROAS drop from 323× to 98× is not a decline in efficiency — it's the arithmetic of finally spending something. Both numbers are total-business-over-ad-spend, not attribution.

**Google traffic inverted from cheap-and-broad to expensive-and-narrow.** 2021 bought 153k impressions at $0.46/click on a 0.65% CTR — display-ish, low-intent volume. 2026 buys 17k impressions at $4.72/click on a 5.11% CTR. Nearly the same click count for 9× the money, but the intent quality is unrecognizably better. That trade is defensible for a $1,410 AOV business; it is not defensible at 24% impression share with 39% lost to budget.

**Conversion value tracking on Google has effectively stopped reporting.** $1,364 of ad-attributed value in Q2 2021 vs **$3.00** in Q2 2026 — against a quarter that did $403k in store revenue. Google is optimizing bids on a value signal that is functionally blind. That's the single most consequential difference between the two quarters and it's a fixable one.

**Mid-point marker (Q2 2025):** store revenue $772,911 on $1,088 of spend — all of it **Meta**, with **$0 on Google**. So the channel mix has flipped twice in five years: Google-only (2021) → Meta-only (2025) → Google-only (2026). Neither platform has ever run continuously enough to build a durable learning base.

### Product categories — the real story in the mix shift

| Category | Q2 2021 | Q2 2026 |
|---|---|---|
| **Untagged / UNKNOWN** | $33,909 (23%) | **$353,983 (88%)** |
| Drones (hardware) | **$82,492 (55%)** | $22,153 (5.5%) |
| Training | $15,890 | $8,113 |
| Event | — | $12,570 |
| Battery | — | $4,221 |
| Countermeasures | — | $1,190 |
| Accessories | $8,002 | $184 |
| Parts | $3,977 | — |

Five years ago this was a **drone hardware retailer** — over half of revenue was airframes, with accessories, parts and chargers filling in behind. Today hardware resale is 5.5% of the book. The growth is in the **$353,983 untagged bucket**, which from the live product list is NIST test-method apparatus sets, institutional/HubSpot-sourced deals, and scheduled training cohorts — high-ticket, program-and-standards revenue, not e-commerce SKUs.

**Focus recommendation:** the categories worth building around are **NIST test-method apparatus + Train-the-Trainer/certification programs** (the untagged bucket plus Training and Event, ~$375k combined), with **Batteries/Countermeasures** as the attach-sale layer to the installed fleet. Commodity drone resale and accessories should not receive incremental budget — Accessories fell from $8,002 to $184 and Drones lost 73% of its revenue while the total business grew 170%.

**Two things to fix before scaling spend:**
1. **Product-type tagging.** 88% of revenue is landing in UNKNOWN. Until those SKUs carry a type, you cannot run Shopping/PMax feed segmentation on the categories that are actually paying, and no product-level ROAS is trustworthy.
2. **Conversion value import.** With $3.00 of reported value against $403k of orders, tighten this before raising budget on Website traffic-Search-5 — otherwise the 39% lost-to-budget headroom just buys more of what the blind signal picks.

One note on the Google side: deep-history backfill and interior gap repair are paused by choice while the capture engine is completed, so Google history won't extend further back than it currently does. Forward daily capture is unaffected.
